items.title: Live: No 'slash and burn' cuts in budget update, Chalmers says
paras: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is promising a modest save in the upcoming mid-year budget update but insists he is not talking about a "slash and burn" approach.
Live updates Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option Latest Oldest New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters
Greens leader David Shoebridge is hopeful the week will end with the passage of the digital duty of care legislation.

The bill would put the onus on big tech companies to prevent foreseeable harms online. The government, who needs the Greens to pass the legislation, says its considering its demand for individuals to be able to sue tech companies if they are harmed.
It's one of the four pieces of legislation the government is hoping to pass this week, alongside changes to the capital gains tax discount, trusts and private health insurance rebates for over 65s.

"There's a lot of tax bills floating around. That's complicated discussions. We'll continue to talk. But the our goal at the end of the day is not to give corporate Australia big Christmas present," he says.
"The government keeps asking, and we keep telling them the same thing: you exempt all pensioners [from the private health rebate change], and there's a pathway through.
"I mean, it is a bit frustrating that we've said this now for months, and the government seems to think that there's some alternative solution."

items.title: Union says some Tasmanian public sector jobs saved but new ones being cut
paras: The Hunger Games is a novel and film in which competitors are forced to battle each other to advance within an elaborate game. ( Supplied )
The "work" of choosing which public sector jobs to cut has been done in a "careful and considered way", the Tasmanian government says.
However, a union is likening the process to the plot of The Hunger Games dystopian fantasy.

Almost a week after Tasmanian public servants were updated on planned job cuts, the union says workers remain in the dark and has compared the process to The Hunger Games fight-to-the-death dystopian fantasy.

Staff at Building Tasmania — formerly the Department of State Growth — and at the Department of Premier and Cabinet (DPAC) were given an update on Wednesday about a planned restructure, following consultation.
The restructure will see some staff and services move to DPAC and a new body — Tourism, Events and Creative Tasmania (TECT) — established.
The last update in September identified at least 150 jobs to be abolished .
Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) secretary Thirza White said that while some positions appear to have been saved, others were now on the chopping block.

"But when you dig into the paperwork … many of the jobs that have been saved have been the ones that have received significant attention as to the impacts, such as in [Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery] TMAG or Mineral Resources Tasmania," she said.
The ABC has been able to identify a number of changes, with positions such as a Mineral Resources Tasmania's laboratory analyst surviving.
Cuts to TMAG — which saw the largest public outcry — will impact five jobs, down from seven, including a photographer and graphic designer.

The Head of Herbarium role, which was originally slated to go, will remain at lesser pay, but it is understood that will happen after internationally acclaimed lichen researcher Dr Gintaras Kantvilas leaves the role.
A TMAG staff member told the ABC that while the spin might be that the museum had gotten off lightly, that was not the case.
They said that between a number of positions being frozen and voluntary redundancies, the museum would struggle.
Other roles have been reinstated but on a fixed-term, rather than an ongoing basis.
Neither the union nor the ABC have been able to piece together a full picture of exactly which jobs will go.
Thirza White says the Tasmanian government has not been transparent about the job cuts. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden )

"It's still really unclear what decisions the government has made around what jobs are being cut and what it means for public sector workers and what it means for services more generally," Ms White said.
"We've got a lot more documentation, but to get a clear picture of what is actually being proposed and what jobs are being cut, you now need to compare these documents with past documents.
The ABC asked Building Tasmania for an updated list of the job cuts last week, but it declined to provide one.
"More information will be available once the machinery of government/transition process is finalised," a spokesperson told the ABC.
Asked if losing a job without wanting to was effectively the same thing, Minister Bridget Archer responded, "I think it is … not consistent … with what we mean by that".
"It doesn't mean that it isn't necessary, and it doesn't mean that it isn't work that we need to do, and we have been very open and transparent about that," she said.
"But, of course, we acknowledge that that impacts on people, on individuals, on humans and we need to not lose sight of that."
Bridget Archer recognised it was "difficult and challenging" for workers. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )
Employees who are moving from Building Tasmania to DPAC will do so on that date, while TECT will be created in February 2027.
In some shrinking teams, staff are taking part in "sustainability assessments" and have been told to prepare their resumes for their senior leaders to consider.
"There are hundreds of workers who have now found out that if their job has not been cut, that they are now moving to a team where there are not enough roles," Ms White said.
"They have no understanding of how that process will be managed and what it means for them.
The Hunger Games is a dystopian novel and film in which competitors are forced to battle each other to the death to advance within an elaborate game.
Ms White said the restructure had been so "badly handled" it needed some form of external oversight.
"We want a parliamentary inquiry established now to monitor what has taken place to date, but also how we are moving forward and to review what happens," she said.
The government plans to cut 250 jobs across the two departments, the majority from Building Tasmania, as part of budget-saving measures.

items.title: Ute-sized nuclear reactor reignites energy debate
paras: A central Queensland MP wants the nuclear energy moratorium lifted following the success of an Australian founder's microreactor.
Renewable energy advocates have warned against the high costs and lack of community support for nuclear in Australia.
The federal minister for energy has ruled out nuclear power, describing it as a "pipe dream".
Travelling along country roads from Texas to Idaho in the United States, an Australian-owned company is transporting an unconventional load: a nuclear reactor that fits in the back of a ute.

The microreactor was developed by Deployable Energy under a US government pilot program, set up in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump to accelerate the production of new advanced reactors.
Owned by Brisbane-raised Bobby Gallagher, the company was able to make a microreactor that reached criticality in 155 days.
Bobby Gallagher says his company's microreactor could service Australia's island communities. ( Supplied: Deployable Energy )
Criticality is a key step towards commercialisation in which a reactor achieves a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.
The microreactor promises to deliver 3.5 megawatts of thermal power and can be adapted to nautical environments.

"It provides electrical power to power up to 1,000 homes for five years without needing to be refuelled and then it can just be swapped out after that five-year period … like a gas bottle," Mr Gallagher said.
Deployable Energy developed the third microreactor to reach criticality under a US pilot program. ( Supplied: Deployable Energy )
Mr Gallagher's company is conducting safety testing at the Idaho National Laboratory, with the aim of producing 1,000 units per year from its manufacturing facility in Texas by 2030.
He said it could help power remote communities, islands, mine sites, manufacturing industries and data centres.
It has caught the attention of the federal LNP member for Flynn, Colin Boyce, who has renewed his calls for Australia to lift its moratorium on nuclear energy.
Colin Boyce (centre) has held the central Queensland seat of Flynn since 2022. ( Supplied: Office of Colin Boyce MP )
"[For] the future of the Australian energy map, we need to explore all options and have all options available to business and industry," he said.

"The greatest tragedy of that nuclear moratorium in Australia is that we've lost a generation of young people in our education system who have not pursued nuclear engineering or nuclear medicine or nuclear chemistry.
"We have literally got dozens and dozens and dozens of people who are now overseas learning about nuclear."

The Coalition took a controversial policy to the 2025 federal election to replace seven aging coal-fired power stations with nuclear reactors, including the Callide Power Station in Mr Boyce's central Queensland electorate.
Mr Boyce did not support the policy but said he had had a positive reception from his constituents about exploring nuclear as an energy option.
The Gladstone Power Station is the largest and oldest coal-fired power station in Queensland. ( ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly )
Coordinator of the Gladstone Conservation Council Emma Smith said she was apprehensive about hosting nuclear in her backyard, and that it was not the "right solution" for the region.
"Central Queensland is really interesting in that we're quite used to new projects and we're used to being quite relatively close to power generation," she said.
"We need to be working towards things that will meet our needs now, which is building the renewable energy that we have."

The head of research at pro-renewables organisation Rewiring Australia, Calum Harvey-Scholes, said while the cost of living remained a concern for energy consumers, he could not imagine widespread public support for nuclear.
Calum Harvey-Scholes says renewables remain the cheapest form of electricity. ( Supplied: Rewiring Australia )
"I think getting people to a place where they're happy to have [nuclear energy] in their community or on their doorstep is hard to imagine," he said.
Mr Harvey-Scholes also questioned whether building nuclear energy in Australia would bring down energy bills.
"Batteries are bringing that kind of reliability, that people were worried about with solar and wind, to the system," he said.
Founder of advocacy group Nuclear for Australia Will Shackel said a "huge anti-nuclear disinformation push" at the last election harmed the public debate.
Will Shackel believes nuclear microreactors could help power the data centre boom. ( Supplied: Nuclear for Australia )
"We saw … a very sophisticated anti-nuclear campaign, which included elements of astroturfing, whether it was three-eyed fish, radioactive koalas, fearmongering about water and earthquakes," he said.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who presided over climate talks at COP31 in Türkiye, has previously ruled out nuclear as a "pipe dream", telling reporters in August his government was pursuing "practical, commonsense" renewables.

A now-lapsed parliamentary inquiry into nuclear power generation heard that setting up a nuclear industry in Australia would face substantial regulatory, workforce, supply-chain and construction hurdles.
"We've run reactors continuously in Australia for over 50 years without any significant safety instances. There is no reason why we couldn't have a commercial power reactor system," he said.
"Australia is, unfortunately, going to be a price taker and not a leader in this space."

items.title: Nvidia’s CEO is back – but the turmoil has exposed the AI boom’s risks for NZ investors
paras: John MacDougall/Getty Images Nvidia’s CEO is back – but the turmoil has exposed the AI boom’s risks for NZ investors Published: November 23, 2026 5:01pm EST Jensen Huang has returned to the helm of Nvidia. But the extraordinary events surrounding the US chipmaker’s co-founder over the past two weeks have offered New Zealand investors a reminder of the risks of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom .
Huang resigned as chief executive on November 12 following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of espionage.

Despite initially ruling out his return, Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang on November 23, saying it was satisfied he posed no national security risk. The decision reportedly followed lobbying from US President Donald Trump.

The turmoil sent Nvidia’s shares on a rollercoaster ride. Between their October peak and mid-November, nearly NZ$1.3 billion was wiped from the value of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund’s Nvidia holdings, as the chipmaker’s share price fell about 30%.
Nvidia’s underlying business remains strong. In its latest earnings report , the company reported quarterly revenue of US$115.8 billion, more than double the same period last year.

But the episode illustrates how uncertainty surrounding one of the world’s biggest tech companies can affect New Zealanders’ retirement savings – including KiwiSaver members who may have little idea how much of their money is invested in tech giants.

At its last full disclosure in June, the Super Fund’s five largest overseas shareholdings were Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon and Google’s owner, Alphabet. Together, they were worth about NZ$10.6 billion – about one dollar in every five the fund holds directly in overseas shares.

But this isn’t necessarily a deliberate bet on tech. A handful of US tech companies make up about one third of the benchmark US sharemarket index, the S&P 500. Funds investing broadly in world markets therefore hold large positions in these companies.

KiwiSaver funds have similar exposure. As of September 30, Nvidia accounted for about 5.5% of investments in Kernel’s High Growth fund and Generate’s Focused Growth fund , and 5.2% in Simplicity’s High Growth fund . By comparison, it made up less than 2% of Fisher Funds’ KiwiSaver Plan Growth fund .

For someone with $50,000 in either of the first two funds, that meant about $2,750 was tied to Nvidia shares alone. While investing in several big technology companies might spread the risk, some vulnerabilities are easy to overlook.

One concerns leadership. In less than two weeks, Nvidia’s founder resigned, the board ruled out his return, and then reinstated him. Each development brought new uncertainty for investors, showing how quickly events involving a single executive can affect a company’s fortunes.

Another is how closely these companies depend on each other. Anthropic, the freshly floated AI company behind Claude, has committed to spending more than US$250 billion on computing capacity from Google, Amazon and Microsoft.
Three of the Super Fund’s five largest holdings are partly dependent on the same customer. When AI spending rises, their fortunes may rise together. If it slows, they could fall together.

Nvidia has guaranteed up to US$118 billion of its partners’ data centre costs, including US$105 billion for an Ohio campus leased to OpenAI. It has made no payments so far, but these guarantees tie its fortunes more closely to its customers.

A further risk lies in government policy. On November 16, the US Commerce Department issued a rule requiring licences to export advanced AI chips to five countries, while limiting remote access to US chips through overseas data centres.
Decisions made in Washington can quickly change the earnings outlook for these companies.

Index funds , often called passive funds, track a market index. They hold companies in proportion to their size, so as tech companies rise in value, their weight increases. Exposure also depends on which index they follow.

As of September 30, the index-based high growth funds from Kernel and Simplicity had more of their overseas shares in Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft than the main global share index, MSCI’s All Country World Index .

Active managers can hold more or less than that index. Generate leaned into Nvidia and Microsoft. Milford’s growth funds held about twice the index’s share of Microsoft, with Apple at or below it. Fisher Funds held less than the index in all three.

Neither approach is automatically safer. Research by investment analysis firm Morningstar on funds sold in Australia found many actively managed global share funds performed worse than index funds while big tech shares were rising – partly because they held less of them.
But when those shares fall, as Nvidia’s did earlier this month, the funds holding the most feel it first.
The Super Fund is built to ride out falls over decades. Many KiwiSaver members have less time, especially those close to 65 or saving for a first home.
One step is to check a fund’s largest holdings. Every KiwiSaver fund publishes its ten largest investments each quarter, available on Sorted’s Smart Investor website .

Another is to consider whether the fund type matches the investment timeline. High growth funds generally suit money that won’t be needed for at least ten years. For shorter timeframes, a more balanced fund may be appropriate.
It’s important to avoid selling in a panic. Switching to a conservative fund after a market fall can lock in losses and mean missing a recovery.
The AI boom may continue. But Nvidia’s turmoil shows how, when so much of New Zealanders’ savings is concentrated in a few companies, their troubles can quickly become ours.

items.title: Hospital staff under strain despite roster change backflip
paras: Denmark Health Service supports a regional population of nearly 7,000. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding )
The WA Country Health Service has walked back a decision to lower Denmark Hospital's medical roster from two doctors on site a day to one.
Several staff have resigned since the reduction was announced in October.
Staff are concerned the government is too reliant on the Emergency Telehealth System.

Staff at a regional hospital on Western Australia's south coast say the service is facing a "mass exodus" after health authorities reduced the number of doctors rostered on site a day, leaving workers under-resourced.
The ABC understands that in October the WA Country Health Service (WACHS) lowered the Denmark Hospital medical roster from two doctors on site a day to one.
The move left nurses without a local overnight doctor for more than a month until WACHS reversed its decision last week.
Hospital staff who spoke to the ABC on the condition of anonymity said several nurses and a doctor had resigned over the issue.
"After 6pm, the plan [was] that everything will be covered either on video with the Emergency Telehealth System (ETS) or the phone with Albany," they said.
Albany is the closest regional city to Denmark, about 55 kilometres away.
Denmark sits on WA's far south coast, about 415 kilometres from Perth. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding )
The staff members the ABC spoke to said the hospital roster change was in place until recently, while WACHS said it was only "proposed".

"A proposed change to medical rostering was proposed, and following feedback from the Medical Advisory Committee, the decision was made to maintain current arrangements while working collaboratively on future workforce planning," they said.
The spokesperson said there were occasions when medical support for smaller country hospitals was provided through ETS.
The ABC can confirm there are several days remaining over the coming weeks when only one doctor is rostered.
Roster changes have caused stress among staff at the Denmark Health Service. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding )
When no doctor is rostered, nurses on the night shift use ETS video conferencing equipment to seek advice remotely from emergency medicine specialists.
"On-site nurses follow the direction of the ETS doctor, no matter what that might be, to save that person's life," the doctor said.
"ETS looks after the entire state, even when you have a category two that should be seen within 10 minutes, you can be waiting up to an hour," they said.
"A lot of our ETS doctors are in the United Kingdom … They don't even know where Denmark is, and they're not aware of our limitations."
Denmark Hospital caters for the town, whose population can swell to tens of thousands during peak holidays. ( ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding )
A WACHS spokesperson said medical staffing at the hospital was "clinically safe, appropriate and responsive to demand".
They said they would "continue working closely with local staff on future workforce planning".
WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat was asked multiple questions by the ABC on the issue but only provided a one-sentence response.
"I'm advised by WACHS that medical staffing at Denmark Health Service is clinically safe, appropriate and responsive to demand," she said.

items.title: RBI issues Draft Amendment Directions for ‘Preventive Safeguards for Electronic Banking Transactions (EBTs)’
paras: The Reserve Bank had issued the Amendment Directions dated June 24, 2026 on ‘ Customer Protection in Fraudulent Electronic Banking Transactions ’ which, inter alia, strengthened the existing framework for limiting liability of customers in unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions (EBTs). While the revised framework primarily addresses customer liability in the event of fraudulent EBTs, a need is felt to strengthen the same from a preventive perspective by providing customers with greater control over the manner and extent to which digital payment channels may be used. Further, on a review to bring in uniformity in practices adopted by banks and ensure that customers are protected against specific acts of omission or commission on part of the banks, it has been decided to expand the scope of the definition of ‘negligence by a bank’ specified in the aforementioned Amendment Directions. 2. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has today issued the following draft Amendment Directions for public comments, which propose to amend Directions on Responsible Business Conduct issued by the Department of Regulation, RBI: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Third Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Regional Rural Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Fifth Amendment Directions, 2026 3. The comments / feedback on the draft Amendment Directions may be submitted by the regulated entities and members of public / other stakeholders on or before December 14, 2026 through the following channels: the ‘ Connect 2 Regulate ’ section on the website by following the corresponding hyperlink provided against each document in the page where they are hosted; or by email with the subject line ‘Feedback on (full name of the draft Amendment Directions (including the type of Regulated Entity))’. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1548

items.title: RBI releases 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs)
paras: State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank continue to be identified as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) under the same bucketing structure as in the 2025 list of D-SIBs . The additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) requirement for these D-SIBs will be in addition to the capital conservation buffer. The list of D-SIBs is as follows: Bucket Banks Additional Common Equity Tier 1 requirement as a percentage of Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs) 5 - 1% 4 State Bank of India 0.80% 3 - 0.60% 2 HDFC Bank 0.40% 1 ICICI Bank 0.20% Background: The Reserve Bank had issued the Framework for dealing with Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) on July 22, 2014 , which was subsequently updated on December 28, 2023 . The D-SIB framework requires the Reserve Bank to disclose the names of banks designated as D-SIBs starting from 2015 and place these banks in appropriate buckets depending upon their Systemic Importance Scores (SISs). Based on the bucket in which a D-SIB is placed, an additional common equity requirement has to be applied to it. In case a foreign bank having branch presence in India is a Global Systemically Important Bank (G-SIB) , it has to maintain additional CET1 capital surcharge in India as applicable to it as a G-SIB, proportionate to its Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs) in India, i.e., additional CET1 buffer prescribed by the home regulator (amount) multiplied by India RWA as per consolidated global Group books divided by total consolidated global Group RWA. The Reserve Bank had announced SBI and ICICI Bank as D-SIBs in 2015 and 2016 while HDFC Bank was classified as D-SIB in 2017 along with SBI and ICICI Bank. The current update is based on the data collected from banks as on March 31, 2026. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1547

items.title: Governor, Reserve Bank of India meets Managing Directors & Chief Executive Officers of select NBFCs, HFCs and Industry R
paras: As part of the Reserve Bank’s ongoing engagement with regulated entities, the Governor, Reserve Bank of India, today met in Mumbai with the Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officers (MDs & CEOs) of select Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), including Government NBFCs, Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) and Microfinance Institutions. Representatives of Sa-Dhan, the Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN) and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) also participated. Deputy Governors Shri Swaminathan J., Dr Poonam Gupta, Shri S. C. Murmu and Shri Rohit Jain attended the meeting, along with other senior officers of the Reserve Bank. The MD & CEO of the National Housing Bank also participated. The Governor acknowledged the role of NBFCs and HFCs in supporting economic activity by widening access to credit. He emphasised the need for responsible and sustainable credit growth and urged NBFCs to put customers first as they expand their business. He highlighted the importance of quality service, effective grievance redressal and fair recovery practices. He also encouraged NBFCs to use the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) for customer onboarding and to keep customer records in the registry up to date to improve customer convenience. The Governor urged participants to strengthen their cybersecurity infrastructure and adopt a comprehensive, risk-based approach to managing cyber and IT risks, with appropriate oversight by their boards and senior management. Participants shared feedback on policy and operational matters concerning the NBFC sector. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1554

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: India to grow at 6.8 pc in FY25 and 6.6 pc in FY26: S&P Global Market Intelligence
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): India's growth, although moderating, remains strong with a forecasted average of 6.8 per cent for the fiscal year 2024-25 and 6.6 per cent for 2025-26, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . Despite a slowdown in economic momentum due to weaker public-sector investment, the outlook for India's economy is buoyed by several positive factors. Easing inflation, favourable monsoon conditions, and increased government social spending are expected to boost household demand. Additionally, healthy corporate balance sheets are playing a vital role in supporting the recovery of private investment. S&P Global Market Intelligence has released its October Global Economic Forecast update, emphasizing a steady global economic expansion supported by policy stimulus, while acknowledging risks from geopolitical factors. The outlook highlights moderating inflation and easing monetary policies as key factors steering the global economy towards a "soft landing."

Ken Wattret, global economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , remarked, "The global economy is on track for a soft landing, with inflation rates moderating and monetary policy easing becoming more widespread. Still, geopolitical developments have the capacity to dampen or even derail the expansion." Report forecasts an annual real GDP growth rate of 4.3 per cent in 2024 and 4.4 per cent in 2025 for the region excluding China and Japan. Aiding this growth is resilient domestic demand, as regional central banks adopt more accommodative monetary stances. The start of the US Federal Reserve's easing cycle in September is creating more room for interest rate cuts, prompting several central banks, including those in the Philippines, New Zealand, Hong Kong SAR, and Indonesia, to lower rates. S&P Global Market Intelligence underscores that while the global economic outlook remains positive, risks persist. Geopolitical tensions could potentially derail economic progress, especially in regions with heightened uncertainties. Nonetheless, policy measures aimed at stimulating growth, coupled with moderating inflation, are setting the stage for a sustained economic expansion. (ANI)

items.title: Asia's Largest Mindfulness India Summit 2024 Marks a New Era for Corporate Culture and Personal Well-being with the Inau
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. items.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
paras: Confusion and blame Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.

25 ... ... ... An aerial view of Middletown, Iowa, which sits on the edge of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Credit: Getty | Scott Olson An aerial view of Middletown, Iowa, which sits on the edge of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Credit: Getty | Scott Olson Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

In late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a New York Times report . MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

But two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s plans, the Times reported. The company’s founder said MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response

Now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion. Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend . “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”

The Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Last Thursday, Telle said that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday .

In his social media post Monday, Trump said he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.
In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contact was canceled.
“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.

items.title: Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a big secret
paras: Never A Straight Answer Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it’s a big secret “I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly.”

20 ... ... ... A Progress spacecraft is seen departing the space station in February 2023. Credit: NASA A Progress spacecraft is seen departing the space station in February 2023. Credit: NASA Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft.
“It’s my understanding there’s another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress,” Foust said. “Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?”

This Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch.

“Regarding the Progress launch, I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly for any questions tied to that vehicle,” said the senior NASA official on the call, Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager for NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program.
Effectively, this is a “Go f- yourself” response from NASA. Roscosmos typically does not reply to Western media outlets, and everyone knows this.

So why is a bog-standard Progress launch suddenly a state secret? It seems to be a recent policy change, because, historically, NASA has televised every one of these cargo flights from Russia’s main spaceport in Baikonur, Kazakhstan. But there is no information about the upcoming launch on NASA’s television schedule for upcoming “live” events.

As recently as September, NASA provided live television coverage of Progress launches from Baikonur. It even issued a media advisory promising to update its broadcast schedule once Roscosmos provided launch details. Two months later, NASA officials apparently are unwilling to confirm that another Progress launch is taking place.
The question is whether this decision was made by NASA or was a request from Roscosmos, and, ultimately, whether any of this matters. We can make some educated guesses.

It is probably safe to surmise that the decision here was originally made by state-sponsored Russian space corporation Roscosmos. The company has not been advertising the preparation of the Progress spacecraft as it customarily does, some local sources say . Russian space reporter Anatoly Zak confirms that Roscosmos has “dramatically curtailed” its coverage of all launch campaigns in recent months. There is no mention of the launch on Roscosmos’ Telegram channel .

So why is Roscosmos doing this? There are some novel aspects of this flight. Among the cargo being brought to the space station is a robot that was created to assist spacewalkers during extravehicular activities. Operated by humans, the human-like “Teledroid” is designed to operate in a vacuum, exposed to radiation. Surely nothing will go wrong with this.

This is also the first launch of a Progress spacecraft since NASA and Roscosmos agreed that the leaky PrK module on board the space station would be decommissioned . Zak reports that, as a result, the Progress spacecraft will first dock to the Poisk module, where it will be unloaded. It will then be moved from there to the docking port attached to the PrK module to provide propulsion for the space station. Docked there, the ship’s propulsion system is better aligned with the station’s main axis.
But none of this likely is the cause of secrecy surrounding Tuesday’s Progress launch. Rather, more likely it is due to Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Ars reported earlier this year that, after a spaceport in northern Russia came under attack from drones on multiple occasions, the Russian government put a tighter lid on information about its launches from Plesetsk. It now seems likely that Russia has extended this secrecy policy to other missions at other spaceports.

For example, earlier this month, Russia launched a Soyuz rocket from the Vostochny Cosmodrome without publicly announcing its precise launch date and time beforehand. Roscosmos confirmed the mission only after liftoff, and independent observers had to rely on local government notices to determine when the launch would occur.

Through all of the geopolitical turmoil on Earth, NASA has sought to maintain a good working relationship with Russia. Most likely, then, NASA has gone along with Russia’s secrecy policy for this week’s cargo launch—absurd though it appears in a culture of transparency.

Nevertheless, this kind of secrecy would seemingly be untenable with a crewed launch involving NASA astronauts. The next test of this will come in March 2027, when the Soyuz MS-30 mission carrying three astronauts, including NASA’s Deniz Burnham, is due to lift off from Baikonur. We’ll be watching.

items.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
paras: Consumer Checkpoint Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more Personalized pricing can mean unfair, and even biased, prices.

50 ... ... ... Credit: Getty Credit: Getty Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav “It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.
But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

Surveillance pricing, according to the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center ( EPIC ), is an algorithmic pricing practice that charges individuals or groups of individuals different prices “for the same goods or services.”
“The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains .

Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart says the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.

Dynamic pricing , or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.
While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.

For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target said that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

ZipRecruiter was one of the first companies to leverage surveillance pricing as we think of it today. In 2018, its profits increased 84 percent by using surveillance pricing versus charging every customer $99. Surveillance pricing is still somewhat nascent, but its potential lucrativeness and the growing availability of user data suggest it may become more common.
Other technological advancements, including advanced machine-learning methods, have further facilitated the growth of personalized pricing.
In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said at least 250 companies used surveillance pricing.

According to a 2025 statement from then-FTC Chair Lina M. Khan, “retailers frequently use people’s personal information to set targeted, tailored prices for goods and services—from a person’s location and demographics, down to their mouse movements on a webpage.”

Surveillance pricing has become more widespread as food delivery platforms, rideshare services, rental housing providers, and other businesses have gained access to the technology and data needed to implement it. Third-party data brokers, advertising and analytics companies, and credit providers make it easy for organizations to get the information needed to build customer profiles. The growth of web browsing, the Internet of Things, and user tracking have created data-rich digital lives that are simple for retailers to analyze.
Additionally, the rise of e-commerce means even more customer data is available, which makes it easier to charge customers different prices than a physical store could.

Surveillance pricing makes it hard for shoppers to get the best, or even fair, prices and makes it difficult to assess the true value of products. There are also broader implications that go beyond how consumers feel about it.
A 2025 report from the American Economic Liberties Project, “Prohibiting Surveillance Prices and Wages” ( PDF ), says surveillance pricing relies on biased algorithms :

Algorithms often rely on data that reflect historical and ongoing biases, embedding these prejudices into wage- and price-setting systems and perpetuating them. For example, as studies of rideshare company platforms have shown, riders traveling to predominantly non-white neighborhoods are often charged higher prices,a pattern that mirrors historical residential segregation. And … college test-prep services have sometimes been priced over $1,000 more in zip codes with large Asian populations.

Dating app Tinder, for example, was previously reported to use surveillance pricing to charge older users more money for subscriptions. Tinder denied that it used social or demographic data for pricing, agreed to pay $60.5 million to settle a class-action lawsuit about the charge, and says it stopped charging older users more .
Surveillance pricing also incentivizes data collectors to gather increasingly detailed, potentially intrusive, consumer data, which could be used in harmful or exploitative ways.

As EPIC states : “Consumers are categorized by data brokers that identify or infer characteristics such as age, demographics, shopping habits, lifestyle, or economic status. Such personal data collected for commercial purposes also often ends up in the hands of third parties, including law enforcement agencies, and is used for unrelated purposes.”

Some critics of surveillance pricing argue for legislation that bans the practice or sets parameters about how and when it’s used. However, some argue that legislation could hurt consumers , since surveillance pricing can also show customers lower prices.

Barring legislation, there are things that companies can do to better serve shoppers in this regard. One approach is to disclose when they are using personalized pricing, similar to when Uber alerts users that surge pricing is in effect.

Speaking of surge pricing, prioritizing dynamic pricing over surveillance pricing would allow organizations to continue leveraging data and real-time market conditions to maximize revenue while reducing the risk of biased or unfair pricing.

Surveillance pricing often occurs surreptitiously, so consumers, lawmakers, and retailers will likely continue to be challenged by the practice. Consumers can strive to protect themselves somewhat by setting their own standards for what they pay when possible. For instance, when I buy a new TV, I have an idea of how much I am willing or able to spend before I start shopping. If the prices don’t come close to aligning with my needs, I reassess my options, which may include using an aging gadget longer.

Shoppers should no longer assume that “it costs what it costs.” By setting personal spending limits and deciding in advance what you’re willing to pay, you can avoid paying more for a gadget, app, or service than is fair.

items.title: Alexander Zverev called out for the comments he made about Carlos Alcaraz earlier this year, ‘I’ll never forget this’
paras: Alexander Zverev was once again on the wrong side of the result in his match against Carlos Alcaraz. Zverev was beaten by Alcaraz 6-2, 7-6(7) in the final of the ATP Finals , meaning that he still has not beaten either the Spaniard or Jannik Sinner this year, despite being the world number one.

Alcaraz missed both Roland Garros and Wimbledon due to a wrist injury, and now former doubles world number one Rennae Stubbs has called out comments Zverev made about the Spaniard at the Laver Cup this year, following his return to competition. Where does Carlos Alcaraz now rank among the best players in tennis history?

Alcaraz has already won seven Grand Slams and the ATP Finals at just 23 years old! Alcaraz played his first tournament in nearly five months at the US Open, where he suggested he would skip more tournaments in the future due to the packed tennis calendar to avoid burnout.
items.impact: The Australian also wanted to congratulate Alcaraz on his victory in Turin, which makes him only the fourth man to have won all four Grand Slam titles and the ATP Finals alongside Andre Agassi , Roger Federer and.

items.title: REPORT: Jannik Sinner To Have Knee Surgery And Will Miss Australian Open
paras: According to reports, Jannik Sinner will miss the Australian Open due to knee surgery. The Italian has been missing from the tour since Wimbledon due to a knee injury after he suffered a nasty fall in the final of Wimbledon.

There has been no sign of Sinner returning with the Italian announcing that he would miss the US Open, Asian Swing and the Nitto ATP Finals in Turin. Hope had been formed that Sinner would be back for the Australian Open as he had been taking time to recover his knee and had been working on his comeback.

However, according to Sky Italy the Wimbledon champion will now be having knee surgery in Finland tomorrow and could be out until the clay court season. It would mean that Sinner would be out for nearly a whole year in what would be a huge shock for the Italian who is currently the world number two.

items.title: Berrettini called up, Davidovich Fokina and Shapovalov out: the Davis Cup Final 8 squads
paras: The Final 8 starts in Bologna on Tuesday with Czechia against Canada. Italy, chasing a fourth straight title without Jannik Sinner, have added Matteo Berrettini, while Spain and Canada have both had to replace injured players.

The Davis Cup Final 8 starts in Bologna on Tuesday, November 24, and three teams have changed their squads since the nominations in late October. Italy, winners of the last three editions, have called up Matteo Berrettini in place of Simone Bolelli,.

Spain have lost Alejandro Davidovich Fokina , and Canada are without Denis Shapovalov and Gabriel Diallo. Davidovich Fokina pulled out on November 16 and was replaced by Daniel Mérida. “This season hasn’t been easy physically and injuries have forced me to stop several times,” he wrote on X. “My body still needs more time before I can compete again.” Shapovalov and Diallo were both injured late in the season, Tennis Canada wrote , and Alexis Galarneau has joined the team.

items.title: Domestic abuse allegations against Alexander Zverev: Key dates – updated in November 2026
paras: Alexander Zverev has always denied the domestic abuse allegations made against him. The ATP investigation closed without action in 2023 and the Berlin criminal proceedings were discontinued in June 2024 without a verdict.

Here are the key dates, updated with Brenda Patea’s 2026 civil suit. Since October 2020, Alexander Zverev has faced accusations of abuse and domestic violence from his ex-girlfriend Olga Sharypova, and later from Brenda Patea, the mother of his child.

The ATP investigation into Sharypova’s allegations ended in January 2023 with no disciplinary action. The criminal proceedings brought in Berlin over Patea’s allegations were discontinued on June 7, 2024 against a payment of €200,000, without any verdict or finding of guilt. Updated on November 23, 2026 : according to the Associated Press, dpa and journalist Ben Rothenberg, Patea has brought a civil suit against Zverev in Germany over his public statements.
items.impact: January 16-17, 2024: During the Australian Open, news surfaces from Germany that Zverev will face a trial in May .

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
